newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU leaders edge towards commitment on jobs creation.
newsitem.headline: EU leaders edge towards commitment on jobs creation.

text.p: European Union leaders edged towards agreement on Saturday on incorporating a clear commitment to tackle unemployment into their Maastricht treaty.
Concerned that they may seem unresponsive to European voters' worries, most EU governments want a separate chapter on employment written into the union's treaty.
Germany, which had been a strong opponent of such a decision, said an impulse in this direction might be possible, opening the way towards a possible accord.
"We can give an impulse. I wouldn't rule that out at all," German Chancellor Helmut Kohl told a news conference.
But he cautioned that German support would depend on the language of such an initiative, and played down the practical results of such an offering.
"It's clear that you can't write into the treaty which level of unemployment you're allowed to have," he added.
Diplomats said Kohl's change of heart might have reflected a desire to avoid a huge row over the issue.
Britain remained steadfastly opposed to an employment chapter, believing it would solve little and open the door to undesirable legal entanglements.
"The question is a choice between warm words or a treaty chapter," said one British official. "A treaty chapter would be a judicial nightmare."
For example, British diplomats said some might question whether the EU's drive towards economic and monetary union (EMU) would be compatible with obligations on employment.

With a growing public perception that the race for EMU is much to blame for the EU's nearly 11 percent jobless rate, giving the union formal powers to create jobs could offer opponents of a single currency a powerful weapon, diplomats say.
EU governments have been handcuffed in their economic policy options by their efforts to curb budget deficits to qualify for EMU, expected to start in 1999.

But in an attempt to underscore their resolve to tackle the jobs problem, Ireland, the current EU president, has tried to broker a compromise between the majority which want a clear commitment to employment and the small minority against.
Sensing possible victory, Swedish prime minister Goran Persson, told a news conference that 12 or 13 countries supported an employment initiative and predicted it would eventually be adopted.
Countries like Sweden, Spain and Portugal have long championed the idea of a more explicit commitment to jobs growth.
But even among this group, there is apparent recognition that much of the burden of reducing unemployment rests with national governments.
In a speech earlier this week, Sweden's Persson acknowledged what many seemed to believe.
"Changing the text of the treaty will not, of course, solve Europe's unemployment crisis," Persson said. "But it will create the preconditions for focusing our efforts."
Any changes to Maastricht require unanimity, and it remained unclear how Britain could be brought on board.
The slight shift towards an employment chapter may have also reflected a growing awareness among EU leaders that they had distanced themselves from their constituents.
This recognition was made clear by several who said there was need for greater emphasis on issues such as crime and the sexual abuse of children.
EU leaders also focused on issues including bringing in countries from central and eastern Europe, a common defence and foreign policy, and the political turmoil in the Middle East.
